name: Wyandot
confidence_why: No description of Wyandot states a stress rule: Barbeau 1915 and 1960 only mark main and secondary stress in their transcriptions, Lukaniec 2018 notes that the archival Wendat record gives very little information on stress and prosody, and Julian 2010, following Rudes 1995, observes only that the accent falls on reflexes of Proto-Northern-Iroquoian long vowels, often but not always word-finally, and leaves the pattern as a question for future inquiry.
catalog_citation: Julian, Charles. 2010. A history of the Iroquoian languages. PhD dissertation, University of Manitoba, 595 pp. (MSpace hdl 1993/4175). Wyandot data from Barbeau 1960.
catalog_locator: pp. 108 (§4.2.1 'Vowels', ch. 4) and 326-327 (§17.2 'Phonemic inventory', ch. 17 'Wyandot'; the accent paragraph itself is on p. 327)
catalog_quote: [p.108] ... reflexes of PNI long vowels have merged with reflexes of short vowels in Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga and Wyandot, and have acquired primary word accent in the latter two languages (cf. Rudes 1995:23). [pp.326-327] Curiously many, but not all, reflexes of words that had long vowels in final syllables in PNI appear to have developed accent on the final syllable in Wyandot (e.g. Hu. / ˈteniːh / 'two' ⁴³⁸ > Wy. / teˈnih /; Hu. / ˈahshẽːh / 'ten' ¹³⁵ > Wy. / ahˈsɛ̃h /; Hu. / ˈxajoːɁ / 'animal' ⁴²⁹ > Wy. / jaˈʒuɁ / or / jaˈʃuɁ /; Hu. / xaˈtoːkẽːh / 'it is certain' ⁴⁴⁸ > Wy. / jatuːˈjɛ̃h /; Hu. / ˈwẽːnaːt / 'Huron' ¹⁵⁹ ⁴⁷⁶ > Wy. / wɛ̃ːˈnat / 'Wyandot'). Shortening of vowels in final syllables and alterations to PNI word accent may already have been present in Huron, but cannot be discerned from Jesuit Huron orthography; in-depth analysis of unexpected patterns of accent in Wyandot is a promising subject of future inquiry.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Only the Wyandot (Wandat) dialect, recorded with stress marks by Barbeau in 1911-12, has any accent data. The sources treat Wyandot as continuing the Proto-Northern-Iroquoian (ante)penultimate word accent (the 'expected' pattern; most of Julian's cited forms, e.g. /jaˈnɔ̃hʃaɁ/ 'house', /unrahˈtaɁjeh/ 'on the leaves', /uˈnaɁtaɹaɁ/ 'bread', are penult- or antepenult-accented), except that many words whose final syllable had a PNI long vowel carry final accent, so that accent on final short vowels is synchronically contrastive (Rudes 1995 snippets: Onondaga and Wyandot 'distinguished by a contrast between accented and unaccented short vowels in final syllables'). No source opened states a full synchronic placement rule; Julian explicitly defers it. For Wendat (Huron proper) accent is unrecoverable from the 17th-18th c. Jesuit record (Julian 2010:327; Lukaniec 2018:24, 42 n.6).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Barbeau marks 'minor or secondary stress' with a grave accent (1915:27; 1960:58) but gives no rule; Kopris 2014 notes only that Barbeau's primary and secondary accent marks are mutually exclusive. No analysis of secondary stress found.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-syllable accent in 'many, but not all' words with a PNI final long vowel (e.g. teˈnih 'two', ahˈsɛ̃h 'ten', jaˈʒuɁ 'animal', wɛ̃ːˈnat 'Wyandot'); Rudes 1995:61 (snippet) also mentions Wyandot enclitics 'that require accented final short vowels'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent as marked on words in Barbeau's dictated narrative texts (citation and connected-speech forms mixed); Barbeau equates his main-stress mark with 'a rising pitch of the voice'. Statement is diachronic/comparative, not a synchronic description; the definitive synchronic treatment is Kopris 2001 (not accessible).
new_statements.identity_note: wyan1247 lumps two documented varieties: Wendat (Huron proper; 17th-18th c. Jesuit manuscripts from Ontario/Lorette QC, the object of Lukaniec 2018 and Lagarde 1980) and Wyandot/Wandat (the dialect of the dispersed Wyandot(te) in Oklahoma/Kansas/Anderdon, recorded by Barbeau 1911-12 and described by Kopris 2001). All accent information (Barbeau's stress marks; Rudes 1995; Julian 2010 ch. 17; Kopris 2001) concerns Wyandot only; for Wendat the sources state that prosodic prominence was never transcribed and cannot be recovered (Lukaniec 2018:24, 42 n.6; Julian 2010:327). Glottolog 5.1 lists no separate dialect glottocodes under wyan1247 to my knowledge. Any catalog entry should be labelled 'Wyandot (Wandat) dialect, Barbeau 1911-12 speakers'.

sources.note: Ch.16 (Huron) and ch.17 (Wyandot, forms from Barbeau 1960) give phonemic inventories and sound changes with accent-marked transcriptions. p.108: reflexes of PNI long vowels 'have acquired primary word accent' in Onondaga and Wyandot (cf. Rudes 1995:23). pp.326-327: many words with a PNI final long vowel show final accent in Wyandot; Huron accent 'cannot be discerned from Jesuit Huron orthography'; Wyandot accent patterns left for future study. Cited Wyandot forms otherwise carry (ante)penultimate accent (e.g. /jaˈnɔ̃hʃaɁ/ 'house', /uˈnaɁtaɹaɁ/ 'bread'). No explicit synchronic rule.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: Two-page first-hand phonetic note. Gives a 25-symbol 'Wyandot alphabet' (10 vowels incl. two that are 'almost always nasalized', no labials except m and w, r 'never vibrant', glottal closure, final h 'frequently nasalized'), then the numerals 1-10 in Haldeman's notation. The only prosodic remark is (reprint p.38): 'The accented syllable and short vowels should be marked; the former with an accentual, the latter with a dot above.' - i.e. word accent and vowel quantity are noted, nothing is said about tone or pitch.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society
